A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CODECRASH using the same core benchmarks and perturbation framework. Their complete text, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison after matching renamed and relocated content.

before.justification: v2 reports original model evaluations on perturbed CRUX and LCB, including prediction accuracy, reasoning-token usage, density experiments, and failure analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark evaluations and additionally reports JavaScript transfer experiments, refactoring-defense results, and new CoT failure examples.

M1.justification: The perturbation-generation procedure is retained; ALL becomes PSC-ALL and MDC becomes MCC. v3 Section 4.3 adds an auxiliary refactoring-before-reasoning pipeline that removes comments and dead code, renames identifiers, and adds missing imports before prediction.

E1.justification: v3 Section 4.2 adds output prediction on JavaScript translations of LCB programs, evaluated with GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-72B. The original Python CRUX and LCB coverage and prediction tasks remain.

E2.justification: v3 Table 9 adds GPT-4o with refactoring as a comparison against prediction without refactoring under PSC-ALL, MCC, and MPS. The original model roster and comment-ignoring comparisons remain. Appendix G's reference to five LRMs is not supported by additional evaluated models in the tables.

E3.justification: v3 makes uniform averaging across four perturbations the main aggregation, replacing v2's nonuniform weighting; uniform weighting already appeared in v2 Table 11. New experiments introduce JavaScript equivalence checks and refactoring controls. The principal sampling settings, prompting configurations, and PASS@1 evaluation remain.

E4.justification: v3 adds distinct analyses of cross-language robustness and refactoring-defense failure, plus new Qwen2.5-72B CoT failure examples in Table 3. The weighting-sensitivity comparison in v2 Appendix D.2 is removed. Individual structural tests, comment-density analysis, comment-ignoring experiments, and the six appendix case studies are retained after reorganization.

E5.justification: Both versions report three candidates for direct inference and one for CoT, with the same standard-deviation tables and 95.78% correctness-label stability analysis. v2 Appendix B becomes v3 Appendix C without a substantive change in uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v3 adds JavaScript results and the finding that refactoring reduces GPT-4o's MCC accuracy from 45.7 to 41.1. Retained results also change beyond rounding: Qwen2.5-72B's input-prediction CoT baseline changes from 73.81 to 74.1, and its ALL/PSC-ALL degradation from 9.88% to 10.8% in Table 5. LRM token counts are revised. Additionally, v3 Table 14 replaces absolute degradation values with relative values while retaining the absolute label.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix D.2 explicitly defines a weighted robustness metric using weights 1/2, 1/8, 1/8, and 1/4. This specific metric definition is removed in v3, which uses the previously reported uniform alternative. No theorem, proof, or substantive theoretical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The central findings of NL dependence, incomplete protection from CoT, and reasoning-model collapse persist. v3 adds an explicit first-benchmark claim for systematically using NL-embedded misleading perturbations and makes residual rationalization a claimed explanation for collapse. The collapse observation itself was already reported in v2.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands the mechanistic interpretation through distractibility, rationalization, training-induced caution, and cognitive dissonance, whereas v2 primarily describes NL dependence and accumulating confusion. It also interprets the new experiments as evidence of language-general weaknesses and risks to upstream refactoring, bug fixing, and vulnerability detection. Most appendix limitations are retained.

D1.justification: v3 documents JavaScript equivalence validation and the four refactoring operations, but removes v2's explicit 20,000-token limit for o3-mini. This omission does not establish an actual limit change. Existing perturbation templates, full prediction prompts, and the website address remain.

R1.justification: The central positioning shifts toward distinguishing NL-embedded perturbations from traditional structural mutations and extending research on rationalization. v3 removes the Naik et al. stress-testing reference and adds Barez et al., Chen et al. (2025b), and Shi et al., alongside four additional code-modeling references. These changes support a revised novelty argument, beyond bibliographic maintenance.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, results discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work moves from Section 2 to Section 5, dataset selection moves to the appendix, structural descriptions are reorganized, and collapse analysis moves into the main experimental narrative. Perturbation terminology also changes throughout.

P2.justification: The pipeline diagram is substantially redrawn and moved from the appendix to Figure 1. The six-stage collapse diagram moves into the main text beside the confusion plot. Structural results are separated into an appendix table, aggregate tables are consolidated, and new failure-example, JavaScript, and refactoring tables are added.

improvement.justification: The JavaScript and refactoring experiments provide useful additional checks of generalization and mitigation, while the reorganized presentation makes the framework and failure analyses easier to assess. These gains are tempered by stronger mechanistic claims without direct causal tests and the erroneous absolute-degradation Table 14. Corresponding per-dataset results remain available, limiting the reporting error's impact; the overall benefit is modest.
